title: CoreWeave Credit Risk Spikes as Debt Insurance Costs Hit Distressed Levels

tickers.name: CoreWeave, Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
The premium to protect the debt of AI cloud provider CoreWeave from default jumped 125 basis points to reach 22/23 points upfront, a level that signifies the company's credit is now trading on recovery value. This shift reflects a deepening lack of confidence in the company's ability to repay creditors in full, with some market indicators now pricing in a 62% chance of default. The spike follows a period of extreme volatility for the firm's bonds, some of which have recently traded at yields exceeding 17% and prices as low as 73 cents on the dollar.

The distress at CoreWeave mirrors a broader credit squeeze across the AI infrastructure sector, where a Goldman Sachs basket of data center credit default swaps recently hit a record high above 500 points. Lenders have become more selective as AI-related debt issuance climbed to $655 billion in 2026, pushing the cost of capital for many data center projects above 10% a year. While Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the government is monitoring the trend and sees no immediate cause for concern, market analysts warn that proposed restrictions on data center construction in states such as Texas, Ohio, and Georgia could jeopardize up to 30% of planned capacity additions by 2028.

CoreWeave bonds are COLLAPSING:

CoreWeave bonds fell as low as 78 cents on the dollar, while its 2031 unsecured debt traded at 79.5 cents, implying discounts exceeding 20% to face value.

Its 2030 and 2032 bonds also plunged, with yields exceeding 15%, levels widely associated with distressed debt.

Investors are dumping the bonds as CoreWeave takes on more debt to finance its costly data-center expansion, while rising interest expenses and uncertain AI returns raise concerns about its ability to repay creditors.

The selloff intensified following victories by candidates advocating restrictions on data-center construction, including Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has called for an immediate moratorium.

Incoming governors in Ohio and Georgia have also supported slowing data-center development.

Meanwhile, CoreWeave says it does not expect these political changes to affect existing customer commitments or its backlog.

Meanwhile, shares dropped -9.9% on Wednesday, to $48.42, their lowest closing level since May 2025, 

The data center trade is facing a brutal reality check.

selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
A $22B hedge fund is getting absolutely HAMMERED and what’s happening behind the scenes is even more concerning.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Arini Capital Management has been forced to sell roughly $800 MILLION worth of debt holdings in recent weeks after suffering massive losses and facing margin calls from its banks. For some context, Arini’s flagship fund manages approximately $7 billion and was already down more than 20% this year as of mid-October, with losses reportedly getting even worse toward the end of the month.

So what went wrong?

Arini made some aggressive bets on distressed debt, essentially lending to or buying the debt of financially struggling companies at discounted prices, hoping to make substantial profits when those companies recovered or restructured. A lot of those bets were concentrated in telecommunications companies like Altice, Optimum, Virgin Media, and Brightspeed. The problem is that many of these companies are drowning in debt, facing enormous financing pressures, and, in some cases, potentially heading toward bankruptcy.

And here’s where things get REALLY ugly.
Arini was using leverage, meaning it had borrowed money or taken on leveraged exposure to amplify its investment returns. As the value of its positions declined, banks started demanding additional collateral through margin calls.
That means Arini couldn’t necessarily afford to just sit around and wait for these investments to recover. It had to raise cash, including by selling investments that were easier to unload.
This can create a dangerous cycle. Investments lose value, banks demand more collateral, funds are forced to sell assets, and those sales can put even more downward pressure on prices. If enough highly leveraged funds are holding similar positions, the selling can spread throughout the credit market.

And that’s what I find particularly concerning about this entire situation. We’re seeing growing signs of stress in lower quality corporate debt, especially among companies that borrowed heavily when financing was cheap and are now struggling with higher interest costs, weaker fundamentals, and refinancing risks. This doesn’t automatically mean we’re heading toward another 2008 financial crisis. But it’s a reminder that some of the biggest problems in financial markets don’t necessarily start with stocks. They can start in credit markets, where leverage, liquidity problems, and forced selling can quickly turn manageable losses into something much bigger.

selectedTweets.bestBit: At least 18 data center deals now have to pay lenders more than 10% a year
selectedTweets.text:
🦔Bloomberg talked to more than 30 bankers and money managers who finance AI data centers, and all of them said raising money has gotten much harder in just a few months. At least 18 data center deals now have to pay lenders more than 10% a year. The cost of insuring Oracle, SpaceX and Meta debt against default hit records last week.

My Take
For two years the hard limit on AI was physical, mostly power and grid connections. Now money is short too. Banks are close to the most they’ll lend to this sector, and some insurers that take on part of the risk say they’re already full. Some tenants can walk away if a data center opens 90 to 180 days late, and Oracle already filed a force majeure notice to put off payments on a delayed site in New Mexico. Lenders thought a big tech tenant guaranteed the payments, and in some deals a construction delay is enough to undo that.

The biggest tech companies will still get loans because lenders trust their balance sheets. The smaller GPU rental companies won’t. Expect more AI firms to sell stock for cash instead, which shrinks every existing shareholder’s slice. Chipmakers that promised to back their customers’ debt take on more of the risk, and Nvidia’s default insurance hit a record too. New deals at these higher rates also push down the price of older AI bonds, which bond funds and insurers hold for a lot of people’s retirement.
